Brian2 Comparison#

#exp111 · Gamma-gated sparsity · data v35.4.0
Created 2 Sep 26, 12:00 am
Updated 2 Sep 26

Abstract#

We tested whether the snnsim mechanisms supporting the gamma-gated-sparsity manuscript survive reimplementation in Brian2.[1] The checks moved from isolated neuron and synapse dynamics through reduced PING circuits to retained trained networks.

Primitive and reduced-circuit behaviour matched numerically, whereas full-network replays showed backend-dependent firing rates and readout evidence. The comparison therefore characterises where the implementations coincide and how far their checkpoint-level outputs diverge.

Results#

Passive conductance-based LIF dynamics#

We first checked the basic voltage calculation on its own, before adding spikes or a network. Eight combinations covered both excitatory-like and inhibitory-like conductances (Fig. 1).

snnsim and Brian2 produced the same voltage traces to displayed precision; the largest difference was 0.00000000000056 mV. The basic passive update matches for the tested settings.

Threshold-reset dynamics#

We drove one neuron hard enough to spike repeatedly. This checks whether both simulators cross threshold, emit a spike, reset the voltage and enforce the refractory pause at the same moments (Fig. 2).

Both produced the same six spikes at the same times, and their voltages differed by at most 0.00000000000001 mV. The complete spike-and-reset sequence matches in this test.

AMPA and GABA impulse decay#

Synaptic events briefly raise AMPA or GABA conductance, which then fades over time. We sent the same six events through seven decay settings to check this rule without any network feedback (Fig. 3).

The traces matched to displayed precision, with a largest difference of 0.0000000000000006661338147750939 µS. Synaptic decay itself therefore does not explain the later full-network differences.

Event scheduling through the E–I loop#

We used a small loop of 20 excitatory and 5 inhibitory neurons. Excitatory spikes should activate inhibition before that inhibition feeds back, so we checked both firing rates and the first E-to-I delay (Fig. 4).

snnsim and Brian2 both produced an 18.00 Hz excitatory rate, an 86.67 Hz inhibitory rate and a 0.5 ms delay. The short E→I→E event order matches; this brief test does not claim that long network histories remain identical.

Projection and weight scaling#

We varied the two connections in the small E–I loop together, from switched off to full strength. This catches reversed connection matrices or incorrectly scaled weights by looking at the resulting excitatory firing rate (Fig. 5).

The rate fell from 209.33 to 18.00 Hz as the loop strengthened, and both simulators matched at every tested strength. Their connection direction and scaling therefore agree in this circuit.

Matched-drive loop response#

We held the external drive fixed and compared the small circuit with its inhibitory loop off and on. A rhythm score measured how strongly the excitatory spikes repeated in time (Fig. 6).

Both simulators gave the same score in both conditions and the same change when the loop was enabled. The reduced loop matches, although this does not yet test a trained full network.

Input-response curves#

We changed the constant input to the small E–I circuit across four levels. This tests whether the simulators preserve a response curve rather than merely agreeing at one input strength (Fig. 7).

Both showed the same initial plateau and the same later rise from 18.00 to 23.75 Hz. The input–response curve matches at the four sampled points.

Coupling-plane onset proxy#

We gradually strengthened both sides of the small recurrent loop and tracked the rhythm score. This is a simple slice through the wider question of when rhythmic activity appears as coupling changes (Fig. 8).

Both simulators returned the same score at all five strengths. This one-dimensional coupling sweep matches, but it does not cover every possible combination of the two connection strengths.

Uncoupled input-sharing controls#

We removed the recurrent loop entirely, then supplied lower private-like and higher shared-like input. These controls show what the rhythm score reports when recurrent inhibition cannot organize the spikes (Fig. 9).

Both simulators returned the same score for each input pattern. The uncoupled controls match exactly.

GABA timescale and peak frequency#

GABA decay controls how long inhibition lasts and can change the circuit’s dominant rhythm. We tested six decay times and selected the strongest frequency in the excitatory spike pattern (Fig. 10).

Both simulators selected the same frequency at every decay time. The coarse frequency estimate matches, though the complete spectra may still differ.

Excitatory spikes per inhibitory cycle#

We asked how often an active excitatory neuron fired exactly once during each inhibitory cycle. The cycles were inferred from peaks in the inhibitory population, then checked across the GABA-decay sweep (Fig. 11).

Both simulators returned 100% at every decay time. They agree exactly, but a score stuck at its maximum cannot reveal smaller differences.

Selected versus final replay#

We replayed two saved versions of the same trained PING network: the version chosen by validation and the version at the end of training. Both saw the same held-out MNIST image, without retraining (Fig. 12).

Brian2 fired 2.62–3.07 Hz faster, so the absolute rates do not match. However, evidence MAE remained 0.00004 and 0.00011, and both predicted class 4. The decision survived the simulator change for this one image.

COBA-PING endpoint replay#

We compared a saved feedforward COBA network with a saved PING network that includes the recurrent inhibitory loop. Both saw the same held-out MNIST image, without retraining (Fig. 13).

The COBA rates differed by 89.02 Hz and the PING rates by 3.16 Hz, so absolute firing was backend-dependent. Both still predicted class 5 and showed a large rate reduction from COBA to PING, despite evidence MAEs of 0.024 and 0.032.

Post-training loop transfer#

We added the saved PING recurrent loop to a saved COBA feedforward network, then tested the loop at zero, half and full strength. This isolates what the inhibitory loop does after training (Fig. 14).

Both simulators showed strong firing-rate suppression as the loop strengthened, but they differed by 74.51 Hz with the loop off. They also predicted different classes at half and full strength, so only the broad suppression effect matched.

Shared spike-perturbation inputs#

Randomly deleting or adding spikes could create a false simulator difference if each backend received a different random draw. We therefore made each perturbed spike train once and gave the same train to both (Fig. 15).

The event counts matched under half deletion, full deletion and both added-noise conditions. This confirms equal inputs, not equal network responses; those responses were not tested here.

Shared inhibitory-jitter inputs#

Inhibitory jitter moves recorded spike times while keeping the number of spikes fixed. We made fixed-window and neuron-specific jitter inputs once, then passed the same inputs to both simulators (Fig. 16).

Both received 220 inhibitory events in each condition. The input counts match; this card does not compare the network responses.

Timestep robustness#

The integration timestep controls how finely the simulation advances. We replayed networks trained for 0.05, 0.1 and 1 ms steps on fixed held-out MNIST inputs, without retraining (Fig. 17).

Firing rates differed by 0.57–2.27 Hz, but every condition predicted class 1 in both simulators. The decisions matched across the tested timesteps even though the rates did not match exactly.

Frozen versus trained recurrence#

We compared one saved network whose recurrent loop stayed fixed during training with one whose recurrent weights were trained. Both were replayed on fixed held-out MNIST inputs, without further training (Fig. 18).

Both simulators showed a large firing-rate increase after recurrent training and predicted class 8. Their rates differed by 1.48–1.76 Hz, so the broad training effect matched but the exact values did not.

Continuous hidden-state stream#

We presented three 50 ms inputs back to back without resetting the hidden neurons between them. This checks whether both simulators carry state through a continuous stream in a similar way (Fig. 19).

Both showed the same rising rate pattern, but their gap grew from 0.29 to 1.02 Hz across the stream. One short stream cannot show whether that drift is systematic.

Continuous-stream rate response#

We tested four combinations of how long an input was shown and how strongly pixels drove spikes. This samples the operating range of the continuous-stream network (Fig. 20).

The largest rate difference was 0.33 Hz, so the four tested conditions matched closely. Because duration and input strength changed together, this test cannot separate their individual effects.
